## Introduction

This example fits a simple background cosmology model to observational Hubble-rate
data $H(z)$ using NumCosmo. We will:

1. define a cosmological model,
2. choose which parameters are free,
3. select an observational H(z) dataset,
4. build a likelihood and run the fit,
5. inspect the best-fit values and their covariance,
6. optionally continue with an ensemble MCMC analysis.


## Prerequisites

Before running this example, make sure the `numcosmo_py`[^numcosmo_py] package is installed in your
environment. If it is not already installed, follow the
[installation instructions in the NumCosmo documentation](https://numcosmo.readthedocs.io/en/latest/install.html).

This example uses the core NumCosmo Python bindings, together with `numpy`, `pandas` and
`plotnine` for the figures. The optional MCMC visualization uses `getdist`, which is also
used by the [SN Ia fitting example](snia.qmd).

## Import and Initialize

First, import the required modules and initialize the NumCosmo library. The `Nc` and
`Ncm` modules provide the core NumCosmo functionality. The call to `Ncm.cfg_init()`
initializes the library objects.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

# These modules must be loaded before getdist to avoid its side effects
import numcosmo_py.plotting
import getdist
from getdist import plots

from numcosmo_py import Nc, Ncm
from numcosmo_py.plotting import mcat_to_catalog_data

Ncm.cfg_init()
```

## Set Up the Cosmological Model

We use the homogeneous and isotropic cosmological model `NcHICosmoDEXcdm`. In this
example, we rewrite the dark energy density parameter in terms of the curvature
parameter, which is the parameterization used in the fit below. The swap matters even
though $\Omega_k$ stays fixed at zero: it makes $\Omega_x$ the derived quantity, so
flatness is imposed once and holds as $\Omega_c$ varies, whereas fixing $\Omega_x$
instead would let the curvature drift with it.

```{python}
# Initialize the cosmological model
cosmo = Nc.HICosmoDEXcdm()

# Rewrite Omega_x in terms of Omega_k
cosmo.omega_x2omega_k()
```

## Set Parameter Values

We now assign initial values to the cosmological parameters. These values provide the
starting point for the fit.

```{python}
cosmo["H0"] = 70.0
cosmo["Omegab"] = 0.05
cosmo["Omegac"] = 0.25
cosmo["Omegak"] = 0.0
cosmo["w"] = -1.0
```

## Choose the Free Parameters

The Hubble rate of this model factorizes as $H(z) = H_0 E(z)$, where $E(z)$ carries the
dependence on the density parameters and on the dark-energy equation of state. The
observations are direct measurements of $H(z)$ itself, so their tightest constraint is on
the overall normalization $H_0$ --- it is the parameter this dataset determines best.

Holding $H_0$ fixed would therefore assert the very quantity the data measures most
precisely. Worse, it does not leave the remaining parameters untouched: any offset between
the assumed $H_0$ and the value preferred by the data has to be absorbed by $E(z)$, which
biases $\Omega_c$ and $w$. We consequently fit all three.

```{python}
cosmo.props.H0_fit = True
cosmo.props.Omegac_fit = True
cosmo.props.w_fit = True
```

## Build the Model Set

We now create a model set from the cosmological model. The model set is the container
used by NumCosmo to connect model parameters with likelihood calculations. Once the free
parameters have been chosen, `prepare_fparam_map` builds the map from the model's
parameters to the vector the fit actually varies.

```{python}
# Create a model set containing the cosmological model
mset = Ncm.MSet.new_array([cosmo])

# Build the free-parameter map and show the resulting configuration
mset.prepare_fparam_map()
mset.pretty_log()
```

`pretty_log` prints a second model below the cosmology, `NcBBN`, which the model set
carries by default to supply the primordial helium abundance. It has no free parameters
here and is not fitted; its presence does not mean the model set was built wrongly.

## Select the H(z) Dataset

NumCosmo provides predefined observational Hubble-rate datasets through
`Nc.DataHubbleId`. In this example, we use the Gomez-Valent 2018 compilation.

```{python}
# Load the H(z) data compilation
hz_data = Nc.DataHubble.new_from_id(Nc.DataHubbleId.GOMEZ_VALENT_COMP2018)
```

To see which H(z) datasets are available in the current NumCosmo installation, we can
inspect the values exposed by `Nc.DataHubbleId`. The following cell also prints a short
description and the number of data points in each dataset.

```{python}
# List the available H(z) dataset identifiers with basic metadata
for _, member in sorted(Nc.DataHubbleId.__enum_values__.items()):
    name = member.value_name.replace("NC_DATA_HUBBLE_", "")
    data = Nc.DataHubble.new_from_id(member)

    print(f"{name:35s}  n = {data.get_length():3d}  {data.get_desc()}")
```

To use a different H(z) dataset, replace `GOMEZ_VALENT_COMP2018` by one of the
identifiers printed above.

Each predefined Hubble-rate dataset stores the redshift values `z`, the observed
Hubble parameter values `mean`, and the corresponding one-sigma uncertainties `sigma`.
The next cell prints the first few rows of the dataset selected above.

```{python}
# Inspect the structure of the selected H(z) dataset
z_data = hz_data.get_property("z")
h_data = hz_data.get_property("mean")
sigma_data = hz_data.get_property("sigma")
n_points = hz_data.get_property("n-points")

print(hz_data.get_property("desc"))
print(f"Number of points: {n_points}")
print()
print("First five rows:")
print("   z        H(z)      sigma")

for i in range(min(5, n_points)):
    print(f"{z_data.get(i):7.4f}  {h_data.get(i):8.2f}  {sigma_data.get(i):8.2f}")
```

## Build the Dataset and Likelihood

We now create a NumCosmo dataset holding the selected H(z) data and build the
corresponding likelihood.

```{python}
# Create a dataset from the H(z) data
dset = Ncm.Dataset.new_array([hz_data])

# Create the likelihood from the dataset
lh = Ncm.Likelihood(dataset=dset)
```

## Create and Run the Fit

We now create a `Fit` object. In this example, we use the NLOpt backend with the
`ln-neldermead` algorithm. The fit combines the likelihood, the model set, and a
numerical differentiation method.

We run it with `run_restart` rather than `run`. Nelder-Mead is a simplex method: the
simplex contracts around a point and can stall before reaching the true minimum.
`run_restart` re-minimizes from the previous optimum with a fresh simplex and repeats
until an entire minimization improves $-2\ln L$ by less than a tolerance. Its arguments
are the message level, the absolute tolerance (`1.0e-3`), the relative tolerance (`0.0`,
i.e. unused), and two optional arguments for saving the model set to a file, left as
`None` here. On this fit the restart is not decorative: the first pass stops at
$-2\ln L = 248.55$ and the second reaches $247.92$, an improvement of $0.63$. That is a
small shift, but it is far above the $10^{-3}$ tolerance, which is why a second
minimization was run at all.

```{python}
# Create the fit object
fit = Ncm.Fit.factory(
    Ncm.FitType.NLOPT,
    "ln-neldermead",
    lh,
    mset,
    Ncm.FitGradType.NUMDIFF_FORWARD,
)

# Run the fit, restarting until the minimum stops improving
fit.run_restart(Ncm.FitRunMsgs.SIMPLE, 1.0e-3, 0.0, None, None)
fit.log_info()
```

The `m2lnL` printed above is $-2\ln L$, which is not the same as $\chi^2$. For Gaussian
data the two differ by the likelihood normalization,

$$
-2\ln L = \chi^2 + \sum_i \ln\left(2\pi\sigma_i^2\right),
$$

and that sum depends only on the quoted uncertainties, not on the parameters. Here it
equals $233.57$, so the $247.92$ above corresponds to $\chi^2 = 14.36$ for the 28 degrees
of freedom printed alongside it, or $\chi^2/\mathrm{dof} = 0.51$. Dividing the printed
$-2\ln L$ by the printed degrees of freedom gives $8.85$ instead, which would look like a
strongly rejected model; the constant normalization is what makes that ratio meaningless.

## Estimate the Covariance Matrix

After finding the best-fit point, we estimate the covariance matrix for the free
parameters. This gives an approximate uncertainty for each fitted parameter and their
correlation.

```{python}
# Estimate the covariance matrix using the Fisher matrix
fit.fisher()

# Print the covariance matrix
fit.log_covar()
```

The fitted equation of state sits about $0.4\sigma$ from the cosmological-constant
value $w = -1$, so this compilation on its own is consistent with a cosmological
constant. The correlation matrix shows where the remaining freedom went: with $H_0$
free the strong degeneracy is between $H_0$ and $w$, not between $\Omega_c$ and $w$.
H(z) data constrain the amplitude of the expansion history far better than its shape,
so a shift in the normalization is largely reabsorbed by the equation of state.

## Visualize the Local Confidence Regions

The covariance matrix gives a local approximation to the parameter uncertainties around
the best-fit point. With three free parameters we have to choose a plane to draw, and for
H(z) data the informative one is $(H_0, w)$: the normalization the data pins down, against
the equation of state it constrains only weakly. `fisher_border` uses the corresponding
two-by-two block of the full covariance matrix, so the region below is *marginalized* over
$\Omega_c$ rather than computed at a fixed value of it.

```{python}
# | label: fig-hz-fisher-regions
# | fig-cap: Local confidence regions for the H(z) fit in the $(H_0, w)$ plane, marginalized over $\Omega_c$.
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

# Create a two-dimensional likelihood-ratio object for the H0-w plane
lhr2d = Ncm.LHRatio2d.new(
    fit,
    mset.fparam_get_pi_by_name("H0"),
    mset.fparam_get_pi_by_name("w"),
    1.0e-3,
)

# Confidence levels
sigma_levels = [
    (Ncm.C.stats_1sigma(), r"$1\sigma$"),
    (Ncm.C.stats_2sigma(), r"$2\sigma$"),
    (Ncm.C.stats_3sigma(), r"$3\sigma$"),
]

# Collect each border as a tidy data frame
regions_pd_list = []

for sigma, label in sigma_levels:
    fisher_region = lhr2d.fisher_border(sigma, 300.0, Ncm.FitRunMsgs.NONE)

    regions_pd_list.append(
        pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "H0": np.array(fisher_region.p1.dup_array()),
                "w": np.array(fisher_region.p2.dup_array()),
                "sigma": label,
            }
        )
    )

regions_pd = pd.concat(regions_pd_list)
best_fit_pd = pd.DataFrame({"H0": [cosmo["H0"]], "w": [cosmo["w"]]})

(
    ggplot(regions_pd, aes("H0", "w", color="sigma"))
    + geom_path()
    + geom_point(
        data=best_fit_pd, mapping=aes("H0", "w"), inherit_aes=False, size=3
    )
    + labs(x=r"$H_0$ [km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$]", y=r"$w$", color="Confidence")
    + doc_theme()
)
```

These borders are the Gaussian approximation to the likelihood around the best fit, not
the likelihood itself; the [SNIa + BAO example](rg_snia_bao.qmd) draws both and shows how
far apart they can be. Here the $2\sigma$ and $3\sigma$ borders cross $w = 0$ into a
region the model's parameter bounds exclude --- $w$ is restricted to $[-5, 0]$ --- because
the Gaussian approximation is unaware of those bounds, whereas the sampler below respects
them.

## Visualize the Best-Fit Expansion History

After the fit, the cosmological model contains the best-fit values of the free
parameters. We can use it to evaluate the Hubble parameter $H(z)$ over a range of
redshifts and compare the resulting curve with the selected observational data.

```{python}
# | label: fig-hz-best-fit
# | fig-cap: Best-fit Hubble parameter compared with the selected H(z) data.
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

# Redshift grid and the best-fit expansion history, H(z) = H0 sqrt(E2(z))
z_a = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0, 200)
Hz_a = np.array([cosmo.H0() * np.sqrt(cosmo.E2(z)) for z in z_a])

model_pd = pd.DataFrame({"z": z_a, "Hz": Hz_a})

# The selected dataset as a tidy data frame with one-sigma error bars
data_pd = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "z": np.array(z_data.dup_array()),
        "Hz": np.array(h_data.dup_array()),
        "sigma": np.array(sigma_data.dup_array()),
    }
)
data_pd["Hz_lower"] = data_pd["Hz"] - data_pd["sigma"]
data_pd["Hz_upper"] = data_pd["Hz"] + data_pd["sigma"]

(
    ggplot(data_pd, aes("z", "Hz"))
    + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin="Hz_lower", ymax="Hz_upper"), width=0.02)
    + geom_point(size=1.5)
    + geom_line(
        data=model_pd, mapping=aes("z", "Hz"), inherit_aes=False, color="red"
    )
    + labs(x=r"$z$", y=r"$H(z)$ [km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$]")
    + doc_theme()
)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Optional advanced section

The next sections extend the best-fit analysis with an ensemble MCMC sampler. They are
not required for the basic $H(z)$ fit above, but they show how the same likelihood and
model set can be reused for posterior sampling.
:::


## Configure the Initial Sampler

The fit above gives the best-fit point and an approximate covariance matrix. We can also
continue the analysis with an ensemble Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampler, which samples the
parameter space around the best fit and provides another estimate of the uncertainties.

The ensemble sampler needs an initial distribution for the walkers. Here we use a Gaussian
transition kernel, seeded with the Fisher covariance computed above, so the initial
ensemble already has roughly the right shape and the chain spends fewer steps expanding
into the posterior.

```{python}
# Create a Gaussian transition kernel for the initial sample
init_sampler = Ncm.MSetTransKernGauss.new(0)

# Associate the sampler with the model set
init_sampler.set_mset(mset)

# Use the model-set parameter information to define the prior
init_sampler.set_prior_from_mset()

# Start the walkers from the best-fit covariance
init_sampler.set_cov(fit.get_covar())
```

## Configure the Ensemble Walker

The ensemble sampler evolves several walkers in parallel through parameter space. In
this example, we use the APES walker, which builds proposal distributions from the
current ensemble.

```{python}
# Number of walkers in the ensemble
nwalkers = 300

# Create the APES walker
walker = Ncm.FitESMCMCWalkerAPES.new(nwalkers, mset.fparams_len())
```

## Create the Ensemble Sampler

We now combine the fit object, the initial sampler and the ensemble walker into an
`Ncm.FitESMCMC` object, which controls the MCMC run.

Two settings are worth noting. `set_use_threads` lets the sampler evaluate the ensemble in
parallel; the number of threads comes from OpenMP, so it follows `OMP_NUM_THREADS` and the
machine's core count rather than any NumCosmo setting. And `set_rng` fixes the random seed:
without it the sampler draws its own seed at `start_run`, and every render of this page
would produce different numbers and a different triangle plot. Parallel evaluation does not
compromise this --- the random draws are made serially, and only the likelihood evaluations
are threaded.

```{python}
# Create the ensemble MCMC object
esmcmc = Ncm.FitESMCMC.new(
    fit,
    nwalkers,
    init_sampler,
    walker,
    Ncm.FitRunMsgs.NONE,
)

# Evaluate the ensemble in parallel
esmcmc.set_use_threads(True)

# Fix the seed so this page is reproducible across renders
esmcmc.set_rng(Ncm.RNG.seeded_new("mt19937", 1234))
```

## Run the Ensemble MCMC

We can now run the ensemble sampler. It initializes the chain, advances a fixed number of
ensemble steps, and closes the run. Each step advances all `nwalkers` walkers, so 200 steps
produce 60000 sampled points. A fixed step count keeps the cost of building this page
predictable, but it is not a convergence criterion: the first steps are still relaxing away
from the initial ensemble and are discarded as burn-in below.

```{python}
# Start the MCMC run
esmcmc.start_run()

# Run a fixed number of ensemble steps
esmcmc.run(200)

# Finish the MCMC run
esmcmc.end_run()
```

## Inspect the MCMC Results

Before using the chain we discard the burn-in: `trim` drops every point earlier than the
given ensemble step, here the first 20 of 200. Its second argument is a thinning factor,
and `1` keeps every remaining row. The mean and covariance are then computed from the
trimmed catalog and stored in the fit object, so they print in the same format used above
for the Fisher covariance.

```{python}
# Access the MCMC catalog and discard the first 20 ensemble steps
mcat = esmcmc.peek_catalog()
mcat.trim(20, 1)

# Compute the MCMC mean and covariance from the trimmed chain
esmcmc.mean_covar()

# Print the covariance estimated from the MCMC sample
fit.log_covar()
```

These numbers are not expected to reproduce the Fisher values above: `fisher` gives the
Gaussian approximation at the maximum, while `mean_covar` reports the posterior mean and
width, and the two separate once the posterior is broad and asymmetric --- here $w$ is only
weakly constrained and its long negative tail pulls the mean below the mode.

The parameter bounds noted at the Fisher figure act here too, and they are visible in the
triangle plot below: the $w$ posterior is cut at its upper bound $0$, and the $H_0$ one at
its upper bound $99$. The bounds sit about $2\sigma$ and $3\sigma$ from the respective
means, so the upper side of the $w$ constraint in particular is set by the prior range
rather than by the data. The shift in $H_0$, from $70.8$ to $73.1$, is the mirror of the
$w$ tail through their $-0.90$ correlation: samples drawn to more negative $w$ come with
larger $H_0$.

## Visualize the MCMC Samples

Finally, we can visualize the MCMC samples. The triangle plot shows the marginalized
posterior distributions for the fitted parameters and their joint confidence regions.
GetDist reports `Removed no burn in` because the burn-in was already removed from the
catalog in the previous step.

```{python}
# | label: fig-hz-mcmc-results
# | fig-cap: MCMC posterior samples for the H(z) fit.
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

# Convert the trimmed NumCosmo catalog to a GetDist-compatible object
cd = mcat_to_catalog_data(mcat, name="H(z) fit")

# Plot the marginalized and joint posterior distributions
g = plots.get_subplot_plotter()
g.triangle_plot(cd.to_mcsamples(), shaded=False, filled=True)
```

## Summary

In this example, we fitted observational $H(z)$ data with an XCDM background
cosmology. The basic workflow followed the standard NumCosmo fitting structure:

1. create a cosmological model,
2. set initial parameter values,
3. choose the free parameters,
4. build a model set,
5. load the observational dataset,
6. construct the likelihood,
7. run the fit,
8. estimate the covariance matrix.

We then extended the same setup with an optional ensemble MCMC analysis. This second
part reused the likelihood and model set from the best-fit calculation, configured an
initial sampler and an ensemble walker, and used the resulting chain to estimate the
posterior mean and covariance.

In this example, $H_0$, $\Omega_c$ and $w$ were varied in the fit, while the other
cosmological parameters were kept fixed. The same structure can be extended to include
additional datasets, different cosmological models, or more free parameters.
